hp-5gj.spoken: Black's bishop on f8 outshines White's, and Black stands actively, but White has enjoyed the time to whip up a kingside attack—especially if the king settles on the queenside.

hp-5hg.spoken: After g3, Black plays Nc6, adding pressure on the center and preparing e5. That move can narrow Black's choices, though, and may cost a tempo down the line.

hp-5ht.spoken: The Giuoco Pianissimo comes from c3 and d3, giving a slow, positional struggle. White's c4 bishop targets f7, the f3 knight watches e5, and Black has to hold e5 while planning against that Italian bishop.

hp-5hl.spoken: White’s space and plans look active, but Black’s grip on the dark squares is so firm that White can’t push on the queenside without abandoning it.

hp-5hm.spoken: Black should play a5 right away to stop b4, then head for Na6-c5. If White goes b4 first, a5 still works, but Nbd7 is the stronger reply, preparing e5 and then a5, closing off c5.

hp-5ho.spoken: The Bogo-Indian exchange variation looks straightforward, but it hides many possible structures. Strategically, it stays complex.

hp-5gm.spoken: White's queen and f-pawn set up Bh6, and Black's castling walks into it. If g6 answers, that pawn becomes a hook White can pry open. Taking the rook is wrong — defend c3 with Nd2 first, then if the rook moves, capture on g4 and Black's kingside falls apart.

hp-5gl.spoken: Theory here runs deep. If Black slips even slightly, the position can drift into other Sicilian lines — the Kramnik or the Kan — and confusion takes over.

hp-5gq.spoken: If Black ignores the capture on c6 and keeps developing, White's only interesting idea is pushing e5, but it's not great because Black plays Nh5, and with the dark-squared bishop gone, f4 stays weak.

hp-5h0.spoken: If White plays f4 in the Max Lange, expect sharp play in the spirit of the King's Gambit. After exf4, Nf3, and g5, the position becomes unbalanced and tactical, with White's king safety at risk.

hp-5ie.spoken: The Giuoco Piano lives up to its name—"slow game"—so settle in for a maneuvering fight where strategy and position matter more than quick tactics.

hp-5ic.spoken: In the Giuoco Pianissimo, Black develops quietly with d6 and castles, while White builds toward d4 or a kingside assault with Nh4-Nf5 or a sacrifice on h6.

hp-5ig.spoken: White often plays Nb5 here, targeting the d6 and c7 pawns.

hp-5i1.spoken: The knight on b1 heads to f5 through d2, f1, and g3. From f5, it hits key squares and backs the attack, a classic Italian plan.

hp-5hx.spoken: The bishop on c2 guards the e4 pawn, a common target for Black, while the d4 pawn often comes under pressure, so White's setup keeps both central pawns protected.

hp-5i9.spoken: White takes the knight on e5, and Black answers with Qh4, hitting f2 and that same knight. If White hurries to save the knight, Black wins material or threatens mate, with the bishop on c5 covering the vital squares.

hp-5hw.spoken: Black’s a6 stops White’s b4-b5 and prepares b5 to grab queenside space. It also supports the bishop if it lands on b6.

hp-5il.spoken: Chasing the knight in the center walks into a tactic — that move loses quickly, even checkmate.

hp-5hy.spoken: Black plays a6 and follows with Ba7, hiding the bishop before White pushes d4, preparing to put pressure on that pawn. A standard prophylactic plan.

hp-5if.spoken: The knight on f3 and the e4 pawn hold the center, while Black’s d6 pawn prepares an e5 or g6 break in this standard Open Sicilian.

hp-5j1.spoken: In this Najdorf-style Sicilian, when White advances e5, Black's best is Nh5, keeping the tension and avoiding exchanges. If Black grabs the pawn, White's Bb5+ and g4 pins and traps the knight.

hp-5j2.spoken: In the Dragon, premature g6 lets White answer Nxc6, and if the b-pawn recaptures, e5 gives White a strong initiative. The Nd5 sacrifice is flawed — White refutes it with e6, forking the queen on e5.

hp-5j9.spoken: In the Rauzer, Black often plays Qa5, a popular move that carries real responsibility.

hp-5jp.spoken: Black's e5 gains space and attacks the knight on d4. That knight must move, and the square it picks matters — f3 is safest, while b3 invites punishment.

hp-5jy.spoken: White's early Be3 is a known trap in the Sicilian, since Black answers with Bb4 and d5 to equalize or get the upper hand. From this position, Black scores 58%, and that makes it a real practical headache for White.

hp-5ju.spoken: In the Accelerated Dragon, a premature f3 before Bb3 lets Black respond with Qb6, hitting both the b2 pawn and the knight on d4 at once. That double attack nets at least a pawn.

hp-5k4.spoken: In this sharp line, Black gives up a knight for two pawns: eight points to five. Black's king sits safer, while White's is more exposed. Black can hit the queen with discovered attacks, push c3 ideas, and target the bishop.

hp-5jr.spoken: In the Rossolimo, after Black pushes a6, White often pulls the bishop back to a4. That retreat can be a trap — Black plays b5, hitting the bishop, and if White captures on c6, Black recaptures with the pawn and wins the bishop.

hp-5jk.spoken: Playing Ne5 too early is a blunder: White takes with the knight, then the bishop recaptures, and if the queen takes back, Qd8 is mate. Even masters have fallen for it.

hp-5kd.spoken: Material is equal, the pawns are symmetrical, and the position stays playable. A bishop faces a knight, keeping things slightly balanced, so at top level a draw is likely, but at club level the fight goes on.

hp-5js.spoken: In the Alapin, after e4 c5 c3, Black commonly answers d5 and then e6. A frequent error is c4, which springs a trap: if White grabs the d5-pawn, Black's Qa4+ forks the king and the c4-bishop, winning material.

hp-5jn.spoken: In the Wing Gambit, after Black takes on b4 and White pushes a3, Black answers with d5, and if White takes, Black recaptures with the queen — a normal game. But if White grabs the pawn with axb4, Black checks with Qe5+, forking the king and the rook on a1.

hp-5kw.spoken: Play the knight to e2, then after Black develops and castles, push g4. This sets up a pawn storm with h4 and g5, while the knight can later hop to f4, and the g-pawn grabs space.

hp-5lq.spoken: White can try c3 as a pawn sacrifice, gaining fast development but needing permanent compensation. The safer move is Bf4, keeping the game equal with no risk.

hp-5ll.spoken: White's most active setup puts a knight on d5, pressuring Black and threatening to trade off the light-squared bishop. Bg5 is weaker because Black answers Qc5, so the knight move is the choice.

hp-5l9.spoken: Black's main options here are e5, c5, or Nc6. Pushing e5 creates a structure like the Benoni, where White wants to hold a pawn on e5 and keep pressure on d6.

hp-5l2.spoken: If White castles queenside instead of addressing the a-pawn, Black pushes a3, then b3, threatening Nb3 to win material — even the queen if White's rook still sits on a1.

hp-5lp.spoken: If Black castles and White pushes e5, the knight often drops back to e8, and Black’s position starts to look passive and cramped.

hp-5kl.spoken: If Black plays e5 or d5, White answers with d4, leaving Black an isolated queen's pawn and White a fianchettoed bishop on g2.

hp-5kk.spoken: Against early e6, Black aims for d5. White meets it with g3, then after d5, recaptures with the e-pawn and plays d4, reaching a Keres-style setup with the fianchettoed bishop.

hp-5lg.spoken: Black cannot play the usual …e5 advance here, because the knight on f6 leaps to e4 with tempo, making that pawn push ineffective.

hp-5kq.spoken: Black playing e6 and putting the bishop on e7 instead of g7 means the long a1-h8 diagonal causes White no trouble, so the position turns less risky.

hp-5l3.spoken: Once White plays f3, Black can choose c6, a5, or h5. The c6 move is risky: it opens the center too soon, letting White play h4 and then h5 to break through on the kingside.

hp-5l0.spoken: Rook to b1 is a flexible waiting move; White watches Black's setup before choosing a plan, avoiding sharp theory early.

hp-5l4.spoken: Black's best move here is h5, stopping White's g4 and starting kingside pressure. White answers with g5, driving the knight back to h7, then h4 to protect the pawn.

hp-5kz.spoken: White's bishops stand active, and e4 offers a perfect outpost for a knight. If Black captures on e5, White's piece activity and central control give full compensation.

hp-5l6.spoken: After Black pushes f6 and White captures on f6, Black has the exchange sacrifice Rxf4 in mind. This position demands a choice: White can take the material or keep developing. Castling and conceding the h4 pawn stands as a solid option.

hp-5l1.spoken: Once White pushes d5, Black's key idea is to bring the knight to a6 and then c5, hitting the e4 pawn. Black also plans the a5-a4-a3 advance to make queenside castling awkward for White.

hp-5mk.spoken: If Black captures on d4, White gains a central pawn majority and can push c5 or d5, grabbing space and creating weak squares like b4. That outcome favors White, so Black usually avoids the capture.

hp-5mh.spoken: If Black dodges the trade and posts the bishop on a5, White strikes with an early d4, cracking the center open while that bishop wanders.

hp-5mx.spoken: White plays Qb3, hitting the bishop and gaining a tempo. If Black captures on c3, White recaptures and reaches the main lines without a3, which is favorable since a3 can become a weakness.

hp-5n2.spoken: The position is perfectly balanced: two pawns against two on the queenside, four against four on the kingside. That symmetry makes it tough for either side to grab an edge, so natural development is the path to the main lines.

hp-5lw.spoken: White's big center cramps Black, and the e5 pawn locks in the g7 bishop. Black castles and strikes back with c5 to crack that grip.

hp-5m6.spoken: If White castles instead of pushing e5, Black strikes with c5, breaking the center. White answers d5, sealing it shut, and Black then chips away with e6 and swings the knight around through c7.

hp-5m0.spoken: In the Unzicker Attack, once pieces are traded, Black's g7 bishop turns into a bad piece, but White's c1 bishop has no clear home, so White holds no clear edge. Black can strike with f5, shattering the center and smashing the e5 pawn.

hp-5mn.spoken: If Black takes on b4, White gains the open a-file, stronger central control, and a target on d6. White can even play b5, surrendering c5 but opening the road to d6.

hp-5mm.spoken: Black's b6 and Bb7 gives White a choice: the g3 setup or the b4 setup. The b4 plan attacks Black's queenside and readies b5 after c5, aiming at the weak d6 square.

hp-5mg.spoken: After White plays a4, Black must answer with a5, or White's a5 leaves Black with an isolated a7 pawn and hands White the a6 square as an entry point in any endgame.

hp-5mw.spoken: Qb3 targets the bishop and gains a tempo. If Black captures on c3, the queen recaptures, steering into main lines without a3 — a useful option, since a3 often becomes a weakness.

hp-5ml.spoken: A d5 push sends the knight back to b8 and then d7, making a Czech Benoni. White gets more space, with breaks on f4 and b4, while Black hits f5 and b5. The a3 pawn backs b4; the knight reroutes via f1 to e3, pressing f5.

hp-5n3.spoken: Black’s b5 is a tricky bid to keep the extra pawn, but White hits back at once with a4. If Black answers with c6, White takes and comes out ahead. After b4 and Bxc4, Black’s pawns sit loose, and White gains squares for his pieces.

hp-5n8.spoken: Black faces a choice: the sharp sideline …Nc6, or the solid …exd4. The exchange is the more reliable route.

hp-5nu.spoken: If Black plays Be7 and then castles, White saves the bishop with Bc2, hitting the knight on e4 twice. Black often answers with f7-f5, leaving White a passed pawn on e5. White chooses whether to hold that pawn or give it up.

hp-5o5.spoken: The queen to e2 is a practical try. White eyes c4, targeting the d5 pawn and the open d-file. Theory calls the result dry and drawish, but it’s awkward to meet over the board.

hp-5oe.spoken: In the exchange variation, White can't grab the e5 pawn right away. After Nxe5, Black hits back with Qd4, forking the e-pawns on e4 and e5, and White has to give the material back with interest—a classic tactical theme in the Spanish.

hp-5nr.spoken: The Open Spanish demands precise memory of forcing lines. The Closed Spanish offers typical structures; here, concrete variations and traps dominate.

hp-5o9.spoken: After the exchange variation, White can create a passed e-pawn with f4 and e5, while Black gets no queenside passer from the pawn majority.

hp-5o6.spoken: Black's a6, b5, and Bb7 setup is a typical Ruy Lopez plan, especially in the Archangel, pressing on e4 and supporting the bishop. The exchange, Bxc6, removes the knight, leaves e5 undefended, and ruins Black's pawns.

hp-5nf.spoken: White’s central plan is to push d5, driving the f6-knight away, then plant a knight on d4 and kick the bishop on f5, building a powerful attack. That’s the classic IQP pattern.

hp-5ng.spoken: White builds pressure on the queenside, aiming at the d6 pawn and c7 square. Black's pieces stay tied to defense, and the knight eventually lands on c5, hitting b7 and a6.

hp-5oa.spoken: White's kingside majority can create a passed pawn, while Black's queenside majority cannot because of doubled pawns.

hp-5nh.spoken: In the Open Spanish, Black grabs the e4-pawn, but White has already castled and can win it back. The position stays sharp and tactical, with forcing lines you need to memorize.

hp-5nb.spoken: Play …exd4. If the knight takes back, Black plays …Bb4+, and after the queens are traded, Black keeps a three-to-two queenside majority — a dangerous endgame asset.

hp-5pu.spoken: After the dust settles, Black has one less pawn but a solid setup. White's extra pawns are fragile, and Black can win one back and equalize.

hp-5p6.spoken: Playing Qe2 in the Worrall costs a tempo, abandons c2, and develops nothing. But it serves two purposes: it prepares Rd1 and pressures b5 so that pawn becomes a target.

hp-5om.spoken: If White delays d4 until move six, after Black has played …Be7, that’s the Mackenzie variation, also called the center attack. It reaches the same position as if d4 came on move five and Black castled first.

hp-5ot.spoken: The Ruy Lopez presents White a choice at this point: delay d3 or play it now. Castling first lets Black steer into the Open Spanish with …Nxe4 or the Archangel with …Bc5, while d3 right away sidesteps both but commits to a quieter setup.

hp-5pb.spoken: If Black pins the knight with Bg4, White should not grab the e-pawn. Play Nc3 instead, keeping the tension and developing.

hp-5pi.spoken: The Averbakh system offers two paths: capturing on c6, or playing c3. Here, c3 is the plan—it prepares d4 while keeping the bishop flexible.

hp-5ov.spoken: The Pilnik and Steinitz variations look alike: Black plays …d6 early, holding e5 but inviting d4-d5. In the Steinitz, …d6 comes at once; in the Pilnik, it follows …b5 and …Bb7. White often develops the knight to c3, just like in the Steinitz.

hp-5po.spoken: Black keeps the queen on d8 and builds with c6, e6, and Bf5, dodging the tempo loss of the Qa5 lines. That setup is solid and leaves Black with good chances.

hp-5p5.spoken: The central point of the Worrall appears once Black plays Qc7 and White answers d5, closing the middle. It mirrors the Chigorin Defense, so Black can try c4 to shift the knight toward c5, yet White meets that with b4.

hp-5p1.spoken: The Worrall Attack: White plays Qe2 on move five instead of retreating the bishop. That move defends the e-pawn directly, while in the main line White castles to support it indirectly.

hp-5pp.spoken: Bc4 is the other main try. Black then picks between a6, intending b5 to chase the bishop, and c6, a solid setup. The a6 plan leads either to a quiet Bb7 build or the sharp c5 break.

hp-5pd.spoken: White plays Nd4 here, offering a knight trade. Take back and the e5 pawn vanishes, leaving a color-reversed Sveshnikov-style structure with pawns on d3 and d4. That setup is strategically rich, not a mere sideline.

hp-5qd.spoken: White's idea with c4 is to remove the d5 pawn and open a clear route to d6. It's a venomous move, often underestimated, yet it leaves White with a lasting weakness on d5.

hp-5qe.spoken: Bb4 targets the knight on c3 to trade it off, stopping White from hopping a knight to e4. The engine prefers Nf6, but that line has proven hard to handle in practice.

hp-5q9.spoken: Black plays h6 after the bishop trade. It looks slow, but it's vital for the fight over d6 — it stops Ng5 and Bg5, which would hit the e4 knight or the e7 bishop and leave d6 weak.

hp-5q5.spoken: h3 is a prophylactic move that stops Black from playing Bg4 and pinning the knight on f3. It also lets White develop the knight to f3 without fear, and top players have used it for that reason.

hp-5qu.spoken: The knight on d6 plants itself on e4, and White's pieces feel the squeeze. Against the fianchetto, the bishop belongs on e2, not d3 — d3 runs into the g7 bishop, while e2 backs a later h4-h5.

hp-5qz.spoken: Against a g6 setup, skip Bd3 — it bites into the granite chain of f5-g6-h7. Put the bishop elsewhere and plan c4 with d5 to crack the center.

hp-5q8.spoken: In this Caro-Kann Advance, once Black's bishop sits on f5 and White pushes h3, Black captures on c4. That stops White from later playing c5 to grab space and squeeze Black.

hp-5qv.spoken: The knight on c5 becomes cemented after Black's pawn moves leave weaknesses, while Black's bishops stay bad.

hp-5q3.spoken: White should hold off on Nf3 here, because that knight both guards d4 and has a future jump to e4. If it comes out early, Black pins it with Bg4, and d4 loses its defender.

hp-5r4.spoken: If Bird's Opening comes with f4, Black can set up the London System with d5, Nf6, e6, and Bf5. That's the Dutch reversed, and Black stands fine.

hp-5r7.spoken: The queen must retreat to c1 to defend b2, which is slightly awkward but leaves White solid, since Black is a tempo down in the London System.

hp-5rw.spoken: The bishop on f4 is often a mistake here — it's loose and hands Black easy equality. The solid choice is Nf3 and castling, even if it gives up any wild attack.

hp-5rq.spoken: White should strike with c4, challenging the queen and grabbing space. If Black grabs the pawn with …Nxd5, the knight recaptures and then takes the queen — no problem. So the queen must fall back to d8, and White keeps the space.

hp-5rf.spoken: If Black chooses e6 instead of Bf5, White still plays e3, but must watch for a possible f5 — that's the Stonewall setup. The game reaches main-line London territory, though the pawn structure is different.

hp-5sh.spoken: Black has played e6, Nf6, and Qc7, but White's development is harmonious. The queen on c7 sits fine, and the position is balanced.

hp-5s8.spoken: If Black tries to challenge the center with d5, White plays a3, forcing the bishop back. Then the knights rotate through c3 to keep d5 covered, and Black can't reinforce it.

hp-5rz.spoken: Black's queen hits b2 and eyes b4 from afar. White has several solid setups, each with its own character.

hp-5rp.spoken: Black's c4 leaves White with no edge unless they crack the position open; passive play hands Black a dull equality.

hp-5ra.spoken: If Black pins the knight with Bg4, answer e3, and if Black follows with e6, strike now with c4. Since Black has skipped c5, there’s no need for c3—challenge the center directly.

hp-5re.spoken: White's Nc3 now flips the London System. White targets b7, like Black normally does. Black's best defense is b6, holding c5 and building a Tartakower-style setup.

hp-5ru.spoken: White often delays castling in the London System to keep the kingside rook active for a potential attack, with the bishop staying on f1’s diagonal and the king uncommitted.

hp-5s3.spoken: White's bishop creates a pin, and Black answers with Qe7. The queen guards a7 indirectly, but White can target e5 for play after the knights are exchanged, and holds a 3-2 queenside majority.

hp-5rx.spoken: Playing f4 sets up a queen route to f3, a queenside castling plan, and a mating attack—but it carries real risk, since Black can strike back.

hp-5rh.spoken: Nc3 is the main defense here; b3 would be a mistake because Black can play Bg4.

hp-5rr.spoken: White’s edge in this London structure only appears once the position opens. Black’s pawns sit on light squares, White’s on dark, making Black’s dark-squared bishop his strongest piece—so trading it suits Black, and White has no reason to avoid that trade.

hp-5tg.spoken: White's structure is healthy here. The plan is simple: control the center, put pressure on d6, and avoid needless complications.

hp-5sl.spoken: A bishop landing on c5 blunts the Botvinnik. It stops White's f4 expansion and takes aim at the d4 hole. That's Black's key defensive resource.

hp-5sz.spoken: If Black trades bishops with Be6, White answers with Nd5, hitting c7 and making it hard for Black to defend.

hp-5t1.spoken: Both sides develop quickly, but Black's knight on f6 blocks the f-pawn. Still playable, though not as good.

hp-5to.spoken: Qe2 prepares d3 and simply transposes into familiar Anti-Berlin territory. It's not an independent variation of theory.

hp-5sj.spoken: In the Botvinnik System, the e5 pawn grants White extra space and locks in Black's bishop on g7. A c5 pawn setup, King's Indian style, is also playable, but the e5 version ranks slightly better for White.

hp-5tn.spoken: Playing Nc3 sidesteps the Anti-Berlin and transposes into the Four Knights Game, a completely different opening character.

hp-5t9.spoken: If Black tries Nh5, take on f5 at once and deny Black any activity. If the bishop recaptures, h3 and then g4 traps the knight and wins a piece.

hp-5tk.spoken: From here, d3 is the main anti-Berlin choice, steering clear of the endgame. Another option, d4, heads to unique lines, often transposing to the Center Attack via the MacKenzie variation.

hp-5t0.spoken: In this symmetrical setup, White's edge is the knight already planted on d5, backed by the c4-pawn. Black's options are the bishop to e6 with the queen on d7, or pushing f5 and stacking rooks on the f-file.

hp-5ss.spoken: With the bishops traded and Black's f6 played, White can finally recapture on d4, leaving Black a lasting weakness there. White's setup is sound, and the g2 bishop still has a future.

hp-5sr.spoken: Black may park a knight on d4, the hole White's c4 and e4 have created. That is a principled reply, and White cannot dislodge it without giving up material. So White's plan is to swap off the dark-squared bishops and soften Black's grip on that square.

hp-5t3.spoken: Black's bishop and queen step out, but once White plays Bg5 the f6-knight is pinned and must drop back to e8. That leaves the knight awkwardly placed and gives White the better game, with Black needing extra time to regroup.

hp-5t7.spoken: If Black castles and plays Nf6, White's knight takes the d5 outpost. Black often answers with Bf6, but if that bishop takes the knight, the c-pawn recaptures, opens the c-file, and White seizes it first since Black lags in development.

hp-5t2.spoken: White's pawn duo on d3 and e4 anchors a solid center. Black's knight on f6 is natural, but it blocks the f-pawn and leaves the knight open to pins.

hp-5sw.spoken: Black aims to control d4, while White chooses between trading bishops and pushing f4, or playing d4 to reach a Sicilian where the g2 bishop stands well.

hp-5ts.spoken: With White castled, Black must address the e5 pawn. The two standard replies are f6 or Re8, and Re8 appears more often. That pick shapes the pawn structure and what White can aim for.

hp-5u8.spoken: In the Anti-Berlin, after Black plays a6, White chooses between capturing on c6 or retreating the bishop to a4. The capture on c6 is the smoothest path, creating a structure where White follows with d3, c3, and then Bxc6.

hp-5u2.spoken: If White pushes the pawn to a5, Black answers with Bxf2+, winning. So Black can ignore the attack and castle, relying on active pieces and king safety for compensation.

hp-5uy.spoken: If Black brings the knight to c6, White's bishop captures it, leaving Black with doubled c-pawns. That knight on c6 is often a liability, and taking it ruins Black's pawn structure.

hp-5v6.spoken: After e4, if Black answers with d5, White takes with the d-pawn, not the b-pawn. That keeps the diagonal strong and avoids the standard Exchange Grünfeld, leading to a queen trade and a long-term squeeze for White.

hp-5tx.spoken: White castles, and the game reaches a well-known tabiya. If Black plays Nd4, White takes back with the bishop and then plays c3, driving the bishop back to b6. White’s plan: keep developing while preparing to challenge that bishop.

hp-5tz.spoken: After castling, Black may also play d6, switching into standard Spanish lines. It's a solid option instead of Nd4, and White must be ready. The position stays balanced, and both sides develop naturally.

hp-5ur.spoken: If Black plays g6, White answers d4, shutting in the c-pawn and avoiding standard Grünfeld lines. Black then tries to break with e5, reaching a Stockholm-like structure, but White's bishop sits on g2 instead of g5 — a clear upgrade for White.

hp-5u7.spoken: The c4 square offers White’s knight a stable home, and the bishop on b2 backs the e5 advance. If Black fails to stop that push, their position collapses.

hp-5uj.spoken: If the king retreats to d1, Black has to push the f-pawn to save the knight. After White captures on f6 and the recapture, White keeps the edge with Bh6 or Qh4, since Black's king sits less safely than White's on d1.

hp-5v2.spoken: Black's b5 strikes at the pawn on c4, so a queenside minority attack is the natural plan. Black answers with c6 to hold the line, or shifts the c-pawn if White's rook pressures it.

hp-5uz.spoken: If Black answers with e5, White still follows the same plan—trade the bishops, then push h4 and h5 for a kingside attack. Black usually meets this with f6 or c6, holding g5 and dulling the bishop's power.

hp-5uv.spoken: Black’s h6 often backfires, since White answers with Qc1 and stops the king from castling on that side. That move only helps if it blocks the bishop trade, but White has a punishment.

hp-5u3.spoken: If Black pushes d5 early, the engine calls it near equal, but it's a risky bid for a draw. A win-seeker castles first, saving d6 or d5 for later, when White is already set.

hp-5vo.spoken: Exchanging on d5 and following up with e3 creates another key line. White gets weak light squares, but the position stays simple and equal.

hp-5we.spoken: The Najdorf offers White several major systems—the English Attack, the main Open Sicilian lines, and the f3 setup—each bringing its own strategic challenge for Black.

hp-5vi.spoken: Black has a future queenside pawn majority, one that can produce a passed pawn on the b- or c-file. After trades, Black's king handles White's d5 pawn, and a b5 push creates the passer.

hp-5w9.spoken: Black played …e5, the most common choice here, and engines call it slightly better for Black, though that edge is hard for a human to prove.

hp-5vd.spoken: The knight on d4 is loose after Nfd7, and Black must be precise or it gets captured. This is extremely tactical — both sides need deep theory to survive.

hp-5vf.spoken: White's bishop on g7 looks active, but White can simply play d5, building a strong pawn chain that shuts down Black's counterplay and keeps that bishop caged.

hp-5w0.spoken: Black must play aggressively here, because passive play lets White keep a stable edge. The bishop on e6 is trapped for now, so there is no rush for immediate tactics.

hp-5wi.spoken: Bb5+ tempts c6, but Black can just castle and later play c5 with tempo. The bishop lands on a4, no better than its starting square.

hp-5vh.spoken: In the exchange variation, White ends up with an isolated queen's pawn on d5. That pawn sits on the fifth rank, making it trickier than a usual IQP on d4, since it offers fewer attacking ideas and gets blockaded more easily.

hp-5vj.spoken: After e4, Black picks a setup. Playing c6 is not advised — it bolsters the d5 weakness without pressing White's center, leaving a symmetrical game where Black stands slightly worse.

hp-5vv.spoken: White can take the knight on f6 or move his own knight. Heading to e2 is the popular choice, putting the question to Black, whose knight often falls back to e8 to shield d6 and open a path to c7 and b5.

hp-5v8.spoken: An alternative is Qa4+ and Qh4, a direct attack at Black's kingside. That line is not preferred — Black often neutralizes the pressure, and top-level games show it leads to equality.

hp-5vt.spoken: The English Attack main line runs Be3, then f3, Qd2, and queenside castling. Black castles short and targets the c-file. Theory runs thousands of grandmaster games deep here, so both sides race to land their attack first.

hp-5vs.spoken: If Black tries Ng4, White answers with Bg5, forcing either h6 and g5, which weaken the kingside, or a retreat that lets White play h3 and then take on f6, wrecking Black's pawn structure.

hp-5vl.spoken: White's light-squared bishop works well in this setup, but Black's dark-squared bishop stays passive because of the pawn on c3. The bishop on c1 is White's worst piece for now, yet developing it to b2 puts it on the long diagonal and brings it to life.

hp-5vp.spoken: The Neo-Grünfeld offers White three distinct setups, each with its own flavor.

hp-5vb.spoken: White's pawns sit on dark squares here, leaving light-square holes near his king. The pawns on c4 and d5 need piece defense—playing b3 would only weaken the diagonal.

hp-5ww.spoken: The knight on c4 sits strong in the center, protected by the rook, while White's bishop on a4 eyes b5. Play turns sharp, and White's best is a sacrifice that nets the exchange yet hands Black lasting pressure.

hp-5xg.spoken: In this popular line, Black can try Qb6. White ignores the threat and plays a3, setting a trap. If the queen takes on b2, Na4 wins her or forces a losing continuation.

hp-5wn.spoken: If White plays Be2, Black answers with Bg4. Without the right response, Black wins a pawn and keeps a lasting edge from a queenside majority, so White must push d5.

hp-5xp.spoken: If White pushes d5, Black has a choice: capture or advance to c4. Taking keeps the pawn structure symmetrical, but pushing c4 gives Black a queenside majority.

hp-5wm.spoken: After Nf3, Black's bishop on g4 pins the knight, targeting the defender of d4. If White had chosen Bc4 instead, f3 would meet the pin and keep d4 protected—that distinction shapes the whole setup.

hp-5xa.spoken: A pawn push to d5 leaves the f6-knight with no good home: e4 is covered, e5 is off limits, and pulling back just cedes ground. That is the punch of a well-timed thrust.

hp-5xt.spoken: White castles and the main line continues with Nc3, and Black answers with a6, getting ready for b5 and Bb7, then c5. White's queen has to move before b5 hits, and when b5 comes, a3 stops b4 from driving the knight off.

hp-5xc.spoken: The pin on the knight with Bg4 looks tempting, but taking on f3 fails because White pushes d5 and wins the bishop. Not every pawn grab based on a pin is sound.

hp-5xb.spoken: If Black grabs the bishop on c4, White strikes back with Bb5+, forcing c6, then dxc6. If Black takes back, the queen falls or it's mate — that's the tactical trap waiting here.

hp-5xe.spoken: In the Exchange Slav, White aims for a symmetrical setup with one extra tempo, and careful play keeps White safe while tempting Black into risky moves, which favors White.

hp-5x0.spoken: After Black plays e5, White has three ideas. Taking on e5 gives the biggest space edge, with pawns rolling forward after the queen recaptures.

hp-5x5.spoken: After Nc3 and cxd5, Black retakes with the queen. White gets the bishop pair, but Black holds the better pawn structure and the safer king. White's own king sits awkwardly—kingside castling looks shaky, and the queenside is already open.

hp-5y4.spoken: Black's e6 lets White push e4, but the c4 pawn is defended and solid, so that push gains nothing. Black is simply better.

hp-5xz.spoken: White has already won back the c-pawn, and the position is level. The plan is to develop actively and put the bishop to work on the open diagonal.

hp-5z4.spoken: Black's c5-pawn locks the chain, so White can't push c4 to reach a King's Indian setup, and Black can't chip at the base with c6.

hp-5y2.spoken: White tries to keep the pawn with Nc3 and e4, but that invites b5, giving Black space and a lasting extra pawn. Any attempt to win it back only creates more weaknesses.

hp-5y0.spoken: In the Accelerated Show Walter, Black’s main move is a6, and the engine says that gives Black an edge. If White tries to hold the extra pawn, the structure cracks.

hp-5z2.spoken: Black can stand well in the Queen's Gambit Accepted. Against White's e3 and Nf3 setup, Black either trades off the isolated queen's pawn for full equality, or pushes the play into an IQP position where Black holds the better chances.

hp-5y3.spoken: Queen’s Gambit main lines with Nf3 and Nc3 still see Black play a6. White’s position is the more solid, but Black keeps the extra pawn and develops, with equality or a slight edge still in reach.

hp-5yi.spoken: Black’s bishop to g4 is a common resource here. White has several replies, each with different consequences.

hp-5yo.spoken: White faces a choice in the center. Capturing on d5 trades pawns and heads toward a symmetrical, drawish structure. Letting Black take on d4 and recapturing with the e-pawn creates an isolated queen's pawn, demanding aggressive play.

hp-5z6.spoken: The knight on a5 has the better prospects here, since it can head for c4 and later e5. If White blocks that with b3, the knight can swing back to c6 or hop to b7.

hp-5z5.spoken: In the flexible Chigorin setup without d5, Black trades on d4 to free the pieces and stop White from pushing d5 on good terms. That also lets the c8-bishop come to d7, which keeps d5 in check.

hp-5yc.spoken: After d4 d5 c4, Black takes on c4, and White's usual response is e3, getting ready to win the pawn back with the bishop. Black most often plays e6, though Bg4 and a6 are solid alternatives, and g6, b5, or c5 show up occasionally.

hp-5z3.spoken: In the Chigorin structure once White closes the center with d5, Black's knight on a5 loses its natural square on c6. Its clearest road runs through b7 to c5, heading for c4 when the chance appears.

hp-5z0.spoken: After Black plays c5, taking it is hard, because the bishop recaptures and leaves e4 weak. So White usually pushes d5, Black hits the center with Nf6, White answers Nc3, and Black plays b5 — a four-to-two pawn majority on the queenside.

hp-60i.spoken: On move five, Black can leave the main line with Bg4 or Nc6, choosing paths that skip the standard theory.

hp-5zt.spoken: In the Chigorin, the move orders may vary, but the ideas stay the same. Focus on those ideas rather than memorizing theory, especially against off-book moves.

hp-5zg.spoken: Developing the bishop to b7 looks natural, but it's a trap: after White plays d5, that bishop turns passive, and Black often has to pull it back to c8, losing tempi.

hp-60h.spoken: Black can choose between several solid setups here, starting with the central knight moves or the queen move, and each option leads to a different character of game.

hp-606.spoken: If the knights trade on f6, Black's recapture is critical. Taking with the g-pawn shatters the kingside pawns. Taking with the queen strands it on f6, where Bg5 chases it to the bad g6 square.

hp-5zq.spoken: The knight on a5 keeps watch over c4, a key outpost for Black. If the bishop goes to b7, Black surrenders the c5 square, so White reroutes the knight back to f1, heading for e3 or g3, with e3 the best choice.

hp-5zi.spoken: The knight on d7 is heading for c5, but if it jumps straight to c4, b4 keeps that square under White's control. Another option for White is b3, which stops c4 completely.

hp-5zh.spoken: The queen to c7 defends e5 and keeps the queenside pieces flexible, especially the bishop and knight.

hp-600.spoken: The bishop on b4 looks annoying, but it can become a target. White still enters the Carlsbad structure and plays Bf4, then later uses a3, b4, and b5 to launch a minority attack.

hp-5zu.spoken: In the Scandinavian, the opening moves stay quiet despite the aggressive reputation, with both sides developing before any clash. After the knight comes out, Black chooses between Bf5 and c6, and both paths lead to the same setup.

hp-60b.spoken: Once White plays c3, the center locks solid and White enjoys a space edge. White also leads in development, with four pieces out against fewer for Black.

hp-614.spoken: Black's bishop on d7 sits passively, and the c6 knight remains pinned. White keeps a small edge by holding the tension rather than taking on e5.

hp-613.spoken: The final position creates a passed pawn, but strong opponents will be ready for it. Keep a sideline prepared, like c6 or capturing on d4.

hp-61u.spoken: Black’s structure has holes on c4 and d4, but the counterplay is real. Knights head to d7 and f6, rooks to d8 and g8, and h5-h4 comes to storm the kingside.

hp-61m.spoken: White is better by a point, but that edge stays theoretical until pieces come off. Black’s doubled f-pawns can’t be exploited in the early going.

hp-616.spoken: Black's usual tries to put pressure on e4 rarely work, so the Steinitz Defense is a bit passive. White can face it without concern and doesn't need deep theoretical preparation.

hp-60u.spoken: If Black takes the pawn with the knight, the center clears and the position simplifies, far from a typical King's Indian. White loses the long-term kingside attack, but the kingside also becomes safe from attack.

hp-617.spoken: White plays c3 followed by d4, and if Black captures, the pawn recaptures. That builds a different strategic structure than recapturing with the knight, and the engine calls it a sound alternative.

hp-618.spoken: White has two roads here: push d4 at once or back it with c3 first. Immediate d4 lets Black trade on d4, forcing the knight to recapture and steering toward main-line play. Playing c3 first creates an independent position with its own strategic character.

hp-60t.spoken: White's g4 push is sharp and commits the pawns, handing Black a wide choice of plans. Top players have used this Gligorić line to complicate the King's Indian, and it is a serious system.

hp-60y.spoken: White must play c5 himself, or Black locks the queenside with b6 and c5, making d5 forever safe. Then Black gets Qc6 or a knight to d4, with a much better game. So c5 now keeps things equal.

hp-610.spoken: Black first chases the bishop with Ng4. If White replies Bg5, then f6 forces it back, and Black follows with c5 to close the queenside.

hp-60j.spoken: The bishop on e3 beats its usual post on c1, giving White a real edge in piece activity and space. Black's standard plans no longer work here.

hp-61l.spoken: White castles kingside, then Black usually answers with Qd5. That move threatens checks and sets up Ba5 to swap off the light-squared bishops, handing Black the initiative.

hp-60l.spoken: If Black plays Ng4, White answers Bg5, attacking the queen and gaining time. Black pushes f6, driving the bishop back to h4, then follows with g5, forcing it to g3 and freeing the f6 pawn from the pin.

hp-60m.spoken: With the g3 bishop, Black can respond with Nh6, and if White grabs e5, the d-pawn recaptures. If queens trade, Black’s dark-squared bishop finds activity through f8, c5, b4, or d4 and can outclass White’s bishop on g3.

hp-62g.spoken: Qd2 changes the picture—Black recaptures with the c-pawn, opening the d-file. That clears the way for Rd8, putting immediate pressure on the d4 pawn.

hp-624.spoken: Black should answer the center challenge with …Bc5, heading into the Giuoco Piano. If White launches the Evans Gambit with c3 and b4, Black accepts the pawn and holds it with precise play.

hp-62s.spoken: The Danish Gambit, with c3 after the pawn exchange, is no real danger for Black. Black can capture the pawn and keep the extra material, since White's compensation comes up short.

hp-62f.spoken: Black recaptures with the b-pawn after White takes on c6, keeping the c-file open and staying flexible. This sets up a structure built around the d6 and e5 pawns.

hp-61y.spoken: If White plays c3 and then d4, he builds a powerful two-pawn center. Black has to be ready to deal with that central duo right away.

hp-62u.spoken: The bishop's opening is not a problem by itself, because Black can answer with either knight move and land in familiar territory from the repertoire.

hp-62q.spoken: Black can take on d4 and steer into sharp lines. The position brims with tactics, and Black plays for active pieces.

hp-636.spoken: If Black grabs the pawn on d4, it is a mistake. White plays Bc4, develops quickly, and targets f7. The pawn on d4 is hanging, but White ignores it, continues with Nf3 and castles, keeping Black under pressure.

hp-62o.spoken: The King's Gambit has a cousin here — the Falkbeer Countergambit, where Black answers with …d5 instead of taking the pawn. By giving the pawn back, Black sidesteps White's fast kingside attack and grabs a mental advantage.

hp-62a.spoken: Against the Scotch Gambit, Black's main line is forcing and theoretical: Nf6, e5, d5, and so on.

hp-62w.spoken: Black has three main strategic options: take on e4 right away, prepare the capture with Qb6 pressuring d4, or skip the capture entirely with e6 or g6. Each choice carries its own strengths and weaknesses.

hp-626.spoken: a4 stops b5, but Black can still build the standard setup. If White reroutes a knight to f5, meet it with g6 and h5 for a kingside pawn storm.

hp-62v.spoken: In the Fantasy Variation, White uses the f-pawn to prop up the center, keeping two pawns side by side after Black captures on e4. That grants White extra space and central control, with more squares and more room to maneuver.

hp-62t.spoken: In the Göring Gambit, Black can take the pawn and then head into the main line with Bb4, reaching a position with good chances.

hp-62b.spoken: Black often tries Qf6 after Nxd4, a line strong players have used. That queen hits the knight and also targets f2.

hp-632.spoken: In the Fantasy Variation, Black's early capture on e4 lets White recapture with the f-pawn, building a central pawn duo. Black strikes back with e5, and that pawn is poisoned — if White takes, Black's queen checks on h4, exploiting the weak f2 square.

hp-62i.spoken: Black's rare move Qf6 steps out of theory and can pull White from their prep, though White still has routes back to main lines.

hp-629.spoken: Black chooses between a direct kingside attack or striking with d5 in the center. If the rook sits on e8, Black trades on e6 and recaptures with the rook, keeping the f-pawn to guard f5 — a key square.

hp-646.spoken: The Bogo-Indian demands deep understanding of its pawn structures. Strong players' games mix ideas from many different openings and plans.

hp-643.spoken: If White skips b5 and plays something quiet like Rc1, Black blocks the queenside at once with c6 or a6, stopping White's expansion and leaving White with less play.

hp-63q.spoken: Early f5 is a mistake here because White hits back with d5, striking the center and shattering Black's position. After d5, Black's center breaks, White seizes the key squares, and Black stays underdeveloped with no compensation.

hp-63d.spoken: Black never gets to break White's center, and even if the engine calls it equal, that's a hard position to play.

hp-641.spoken: When White pushes b4, Black must answer with c6 to strike at the center. If White takes on c6, Black later plays d5, opening the center and handing the knight a strong outpost.

hp-63r.spoken: Fianchettoing the bishop and aiming for f5 looks natural, but it’s a trap. Once d5 lands, the center crumbles, Black’s queenside play vanishes, and development stays behind.

hp-63p.spoken: With White's knight on c3, Black's main idea is to swap the bishop for that knight, which buys control of the e4 square for a knight to land. White takes back with the bishop, yet Black's pawn structure stays solid.

hp-63y.spoken: In this Bogo-Indian setup, Black’s core idea is to work the dark squares, aiming to swap the f3-knight for the g4-bishop, which leaves Black with a strong knight against a weak bishop.

hp-63w.spoken: Black's structure echoes a King's Indian, but the g7 bishop is gone and White has no kingside attack. That trade favors Black positionally, though Black sacrifices tactical chances.

hp-63t.spoken: Black’s weak d6 square is real trouble, but if Black can play d5 it dissolves that weakness and buys positional compensation. White’s pressure is genuine, yet Black has the means to defend and strike back.

hp-63o.spoken: Qb6, e6, d4, and g6 all give Black playable options. Qb6 is the most concrete bid for equality and more, forcing White to find precise answers. Playing d4 instead is riskier, handing White more chances to go wrong.

hp-638.spoken: White castles instead of the immediate knight jump, keeping the threat of e5 alive.

hp-637.spoken: Black has netted a pawn on d4, yet White’s edge is huge, with a development lead and direct threats against f7 and e5. That d4-pawn is poisoned, so White must not snap it back right away.

hp-65q.spoken: Black's main move is Qd7, but Qe7 is playable too; White holds a slight edge, yet in practice the position is balanced.

hp-65r.spoken: Against the Bayonet, Black's push a5 is a promising try. White answers c5 and gains queenside counterplay.

hp-64p.spoken: After Black plays f6, White has an aggressive option: the knight swings to f4. This tricky sideline forces Black to capture on d4, landing in a sharp, double-edged position where Black sacrifices the exchange.

hp-658.spoken: The Hillbilly Attack has scored wins even at grandmaster level, so it offers real practical chances, even if it is not objectively best.

hp-64k.spoken: In the Tarrasch French, once White advances e5, Black's standard response is c5, attacking the center. White's c3 setup holds the d4 pawn without doubled pawns — that's the main advantage of this variation.

hp-64y.spoken: If White grabs the pawn on c4, Black takes back with the knight and keeps developing. White’s queenside pieces stay home, Black’s king is secure, and the g5-pawn is overextended—Black has a target.

hp-65l.spoken: In the Bayonet Attack, the pawns rarely get exchanged — both sides race their pawn storms instead. Whoever pushes faster gains a decisive edge: Black owns the kingside, White owns the queenside.

hp-650.spoken: White's queen goes to d4, and Black must respond with f6 to cover the diagonal — uncomfortable but necessary. Then White's bishop to h6 chases the queen once more, and Black calmly develops the knight to d7, reaching safety and preparing to castle queenside.

hp-65n.spoken: The Bayonet Attack invites Black to chase a full kingside assault, and when that attack stalls, Black collapses. Theory here runs on rails, so knowing a line or two hands you a practical edge.

hp-65j.spoken: Black plays a6, the most aggressive choice, favored by top players. This starts a race: Black closes the center and storms the kingside with g5-g4 and h5-h4, while White attacks the queenside with b4-b5.

hp-64w.spoken: White may probe with h3 or g4 to chase the bishop on f5. After h3, Black answers h5, keeping the bishop safe. If g4, Black retreats to c8 or d7, since the queen no longer eyes e4 — the bishop is hard to trap.

hp-651.spoken: White's bishop on c4 creates pressure on f7, but if White trades pawns with exd5, the bishop gets blocked and the pressure vanishes. Bishop b3 is best, yet Black's pawn on d5 is propped up by the e6 pawn and the knight on f6, leaving the bishop passive.

hp-65m.spoken: Theory runs narrow and forced here, so knowing one or two lines earns a practical edge. The position stays razor-sharp, and any slip is fatal.

hp-656.spoken: Black’s knight and e-pawn keep the d5 pawn in place. With White’s c-pawn gone, the d4 pawn stands alone in the center, and Black’s setup is solid, if a touch passive.

hp-64u.spoken: White's bishop on c4 pulls back to b3 and keeps an eye on f7, but that's a pawn sacrifice, since Black can grab the e4-pawn. A bishop on b3 alone won't make f7 vulnerable if Black defends precisely.

hp-665.spoken: This variation sits at the heart of the Bayonet Attack's mainline, and Black has to know the theory cold to reach a playable game. Engines call it equal, but in practice Black carries the edge because White's position demands far more careful handling.

hp-669.spoken: White's d-pawn is the key lever after the exchange on c6. Playing d4 right away allows black to capture and grab the e-pawn, but with the king safe and the rook on e1, d4 gains real force — it hits the knight on e4 while being ready to defend it.

hp-66e.spoken: Black's e5-pawn is what keeps the knight off e6, so black shouldn't rush to push it away—undermining it opens the kingside. Instead, White trades the quick pawn-break ideas for an outpost on e6, and the engine sees the position as equal.

hp-664.spoken: White pushes g4, striking at the g6 pawn, but Black holds the balance and the engines call it equal. White is the one more likely to slip.

hp-65y.spoken: After White pushes g5, Black has tactical ways to defend without falling apart. Taking on g5 fails because the queen gets attacked, so Black picks up a tempo on the queen and keeps the position.

hp-66j.spoken: If Black castles kingside, d4 gives White a crushing attack — exd4, Nxd4, the knight jumps to f5, the rook goes to e1, and bishop f4 follows.

hp-667.spoken: In the delayed exchange, White's pawn majority is harder to use than in the normal exchange. After d3, reaching d4 costs two moves — c3 first, then d4 — while the normal exchange gets there in one.

hp-660.spoken: Black trades a rook for a bishop after f3, gaining a pawn and a healthier structure. White is left with a fragile e6-pawn and a loose king, while Black owns the bishop pair and lively pieces.

hp-66n.spoken: The delayed exchange is quick to learn because it's about ideas, not memory, and the move-order differences matter. Black still has many setups, from the Archangel to the Open Spanish.

hp-66i.spoken: If Black avoids the trade on d4, White could take on e5 — but then Black trades on d4 and wins the knight on f3, since the queen is pinned. So while that pin lasts, White cannot actually capture on e5.

hp-663.spoken: Once White’s d-pawn advances and the trade happens, both sides wind up with weaknesses—White’s pawn on d5 and Black’s on d6. The game stays dynamically balanced, with each side holding targets.

hp-66t.spoken: White's d5 is a target, but White calmly plays Be2 and keeps it protected. Black can't play d6 right away, as the queen takes it, so Black counters with cxd5, and the c-pawn recaptures, keeping the f5 break alive.

hp-66w.spoken: White’s space edge in the center is clear, and the d5 pawn can become a passed pawn later. Black’s queenside majority on c5 and a7-b7 is the long-term asset. The key choice comes on move five: …Bg4 and …Re8 are the main lines, while …b5 is the sharp sideline.

hp-683.spoken: After a6 and e4, White plays one of two main moves: d5, the Reynolds Attack, or e5, the old Meran. d5 targets e6, while e5 is the sharper option.

hp-684.spoken: Black accepts a lasting queenside pawn chain, banking on long-term structure while living with the weak e6 pawn. White's compensation is the bishop pair and attacking chances.

hp-67h.spoken: In the Fantasy Variation, Black may instead play e6, heading toward a French-like structure. The light-squared bishop stays locked in on c8, and freeing it calls for b6 and Ba6, which softens the queenside once White pushes c4.

hp-67e.spoken: In the old Nc3 line, White grabs the initiative right away with g4, and Black has to answer. If Black doesn't find counterplay with c5, White steamrolls him on the kingside.

hp-67g.spoken: Black often plays c5 here, eyeing d4. The bishop goes to h7, the knight to c6, and Black may sacrifice the d5 pawn, ready to win it back while building activity with Rc8.

hp-67k.spoken: White can steer into an isolated queen's pawn with c4, trading a solid center for quicker piece play and pressure on Black's setup.

hp-67c.spoken: White claims more space in the Advanced Caro-Kann, aiming to push forward, but Black's bishop sits outside the pawn chain on f5, yielding a better French structure.

hp-67j.spoken: White takes an isolated queen's pawn here, trading a solid center for piece activity and pressure. Black usually answers with Nf6 to hold d5, though capturing the pawn is also playable.

hp-67m.spoken: White usually gets more space and active pieces in the Caro-Kann, but if Black stays flexible through the opening, the tables often turn and Black may even end up with the engine's blessing.

hp-67l.spoken: If Black answers Nc3 with …g6 instead of capturing the pawn, it’s a surprise weapon that can lead to sharp play, though White simply pushes e5 and takes more space.

hp-689.spoken: Castling is the priority here, even at the cost of material. Trying to hold those pawns only leaves the king exposed.

hp-67y.spoken: White’s central pawn mass faces Black’s queenside majority, and the d4-pawn is the clear target. Yet White’s extra space fuels attacking chances.

hp-68d.spoken: If White moves the other knight, Black simply plays Be7 and castles. The pawn on e5 controls f4 and d4, so the knight on b3 has no good squares and stays poorly placed.

hp-68a.spoken: Black often comes out a pawn up in the Meran Semi-Slav, but the price is an awkward king and pieces sitting on odd squares. That’s the normal imbalance in this line.

hp-68c.spoken: After White's knight retreats to b3, it's offside—no longer pressuring d5 or supporting the center. Black just develops the bishop and castles, reaching a comfortable position, and can even claim a slight edge if White sits back.

hp-67u.spoken: Against Bishop e2, Black plays Bishop b7, then a6 and c5, reaching main-line setups. If White answers Bishop e7, Black skips c5 and a6, playing b4 instead, as if the bishop stood on b3.

hp-68t.spoken: White's c4 targets d5, where Black's backward d6-pawn leaves a permanent hole. The whole battle centers on d4 and d5.

hp-699.spoken: The main line with h4 gets extremely complicated, and the statistics favor Black, so White doesn't want that.

hp-690.spoken: In the Queen c2 variation, play turns sharp and forced, and both sides must know the theory cold. The line leaves a material imbalance and, with best play, often ends in a draw.

hp-68y.spoken: Black's strongest move is d5, striking the center and trimming White's edge. If Black instead plays Be7, White gains a pleasant position with extra space and easier piece play.

hp-68q.spoken: Once White pushes c4, Black's b5 is off the table. So Black develops with Be6 or strikes with f5 right away — the immediate f5 is the sharper path, giving Black active pieces and real attacking chances.

hp-691.spoken: White has grabbed a pawn for the moment, but Black can win it back or seize the initiative. The position is rich and sharp, with Black’s activity and attacking chances giving full compensation.

hp-69f.spoken: After Re1, Black’s standard reply is Bg4, and if White plays c3, the f5 break becomes a real headache—it dulls the bishop on d3 and props up the knight on e4.

hp-69p.spoken: With the e-pawn gone, Black's king often stays stuck in the center, making castling hard. Black must strike fast with something like Ng4, though that carries real risk.

hp-68z.spoken: White’s c4 meets c6, and Black sidesteps the knight to c6, keeping c6 or c5 open. The result is a solid yet slightly passive setup.

hp-69b.spoken: Black’s plan is to pull pieces back to odd squares, like the bishop to e8, to support the strong knight on e4. That setup is very solid and tough for White to dismantle.

hp-68o.spoken: In the Kalashnikov, Black often pushes a5 to grab space and set up b5. If White answers c4, Black should not take back on b5 — instead, develop and castle, giving up a pawn for active play.

hp-69a.spoken: Statistics favor Black and engines call this equal or better for Black, so the position is complex but not dangerous for Black.

hp-68s.spoken: If White later plays Bg5, Black can take that bishop with the knight on f6. The knight would otherwise sit passively, so trading it for White's active bishop is the way to go.

hp-68j.spoken: White's knight took a scenic route to a3, but it now controls d5 and eyes the backward d6 pawn. Those two features define White's play in the Kalashnikov.

hp-697.spoken: Objectively second-best moves in these sharp lines are many, and they can confuse even when they are not truly best.

hp-69i.spoken: White’s bishop on d3 is shut in, and the real headache is that knight on e4. Pushing the f-pawn to kick it runs into the c6 knight taking it, so White’s structure looks shaky.

hp-69m.spoken: The exchange-up position after that sequence favors White, but Black's passed a-pawn keeps the game imbalanced and playable.

hp-698.spoken: White can pick Queen c2 or Rook e1 here. The Rook e1 line, the Staunton, gives White a nice outpost on e5 and leaves Black's pieces squeezed along the first two ranks.

hp-6aj.spoken: Black must not trade pawns on d4, because that lets White bring the knight to c3 and keep a wide center. Instead, play Bb6 and hold the tension.

hp-6at.spoken: If White plays d3, Black should respond with h6 to stop Bg5. That setup is less active, so Black develops comfortably with Bb7 or d6.

hp-6aa.spoken: The bishop on c5 bears down on f2, creating tactical chances like sacrifices on that square. That pressure is why this line is so venomous.

hp-6ah.spoken: After White pushes a4, the pawn on b5 is under fire and the rook on a8 sits undefended. Black often slips by chasing the e4 pawn, but that move loses.

hp-6b1.spoken: White can strike with f4, building a sharp attacking formation much like the Vienna Gambit. The quieter option is Bf4, putting pressure on e5 and possibly luring Black into surrendering the bishop pair.

hp-6an.spoken: Against Re1, Black has no reason to chase knight g4 tricks. Simple d6 with normal development equalizes without trouble — Re1 is just not a critical line.

hp-6ab.spoken: The Neo-Arkhangelsk has earned its place at the top level, played by Anand, Caruana, and Carlsen. Nineteenth-century players misunderstood it, but modern practice reveals real dynamic pressure for Black.

hp-6a5.spoken: White has a strong move here: Bg5. It guards the f2 pawn and keeps the pin on Black's knight, so Black cannot break it with f6. The rook stays pinned, and White can now attack the pinned piece.

hp-6a4.spoken: Black's bishop on b4 is exposed, so White keeps pressure with Bg5, chasing the queen to e8 and clearing the way for Rc1 with threats.

hp-6b0.spoken: The alternative Bf4 is also threatening, hitting e5 hard. Black answers with c5 or castles. If Black castles, White avoids trading on e5—that would be poor. Instead, White pushes d5, and if Black captures, the position levels out.

hp-6ad.spoken: White can also play d3, shielding e4, and then bring the knight out, setting up Bg5. If Black answers with h6, White takes on f6 and ruins Black's pawns. That proves the bishop on c5 can stay weak for a long time.

hp-6a8.spoken: In the Neo-Arkhangelsk, Black's bishop on c5 eyes f2 and leaves the c8-bishop free, unlike the Archangel where it commits to b7. That flexibility lets Black pick a setup based on White's moves.

hp-6b2.spoken: Black's bishop on e6 is the more active choice, because it backs the d5 break.

hp-6ap.spoken: If Black tries c5 after f4, White answers Qc3, and if Black pushes c4, the knight on e5 hangs, so White wins a piece. Black’s better plan is Nc6 and castling.

hp-6bq.spoken: Black's bishop on g7 anchors the defense. If White plants a pawn on e5 to close that diagonal, White's own bishop grows stronger.

hp-6bf.spoken: Watch for Black's e5 or f5 — either one opens the kingside and gains activity. White skips castling here and plays d5 or h3 instead.

hp-6c4.spoken: If Black castles kingside here, White gets a clear target. Play g3, then f4, to undermine the g-pawn and bring the rooks to the h-file for the attack.

hp-6ba.spoken: White's knight on d4 is a real thorn, so White often trades the bishop for it. After exd4, the knight slides back to e2, keeping d4 safe.

hp-6b8.spoken: Black’s d6-pawn is backward, just like in many Sicilian structures. The plan is to fix it with a pawn on d5, blockade it, and then pile on the pressure.

hp-6bs.spoken: In the c6 line, Black leaves d5 and the c4 pawn as targets. White can bring a knight to d4, eyeing c4, and then pile up on it to fix it.

hp-6bo.spoken: The Kholmov System gets less respect than it deserves, and it shines in blitz—the defender rarely finds the precise moves under time pressure.

hp-6bc.spoken: If Black misses b5, White plays c4 and then Nd5, turning the knight into a strong piece against a bad bishop. The queen and bishop together control h6, boxing in Black's options.

hp-6c2.spoken: White's pieces sit well here: the bishop on b5 outclasses Black's on d7, and the rooks and queen hold more activity, even though the knight on f3 lags behind the bishop on g7.

hp-6bn.spoken: White's bishop and queen on the kingside signal the coming attack, and White stands ready to give up material for a dangerous initiative.

hp-6cc.spoken: After …d6, capturing on d6 gives Black central counterplay. The flank strike …b6, attacking the pawn chain, is the more practical choice for Black despite what the engine says.

hp-6ci.spoken: Black's main move here is Nb8-d7, while White often plays a4 to gain queenside space. This known tabiya frequently ends in draws, though practical chances exist for both sides.

hp-6bp.spoken: White's d4, e4, and f4 pawns build a large center and grant extra space. Once Black's bishop reaches b7, development is equal, but that central pawn mass stays a long-term advantage.

hp-6b9.spoken: Black contests d5 to keep White's knight from settling there. The b3 and c4 setup is too slow, since it surrenders d4 and b4.

hp-6br.spoken: After Black pushes c5 and then c4, he grabs queenside space but loses central influence, since that pawn stops pressuring White's center. White answers by slamming d5 and lining up e5.

hp-6bb.spoken: Once the c-pawns come off, White is left with a backward pawn on c2, while Black keeps the bishop pair—that can sting. The engine says equal, but for a human White has no obvious plan.

hp-6c6.spoken: Wait for Black to play e6, protecting the knight and building a solid setup. A common alternative is c6, defending the knight too. After c6, White plays Bc4, saving d4 for later.

hp-6c0.spoken: In the main line, Black often chases the bishop with h6 and then g5, pushing it back to g3. That is Black’s best try, but it usually leads to queenside castling, which hurts because it blocks the c6-b5 and c5 pawn breaks.

hp-6bd.spoken: White castles kingside and expands with f4, steering the attack at Black's king—the standard Pirc plan.

hp-6c5.spoken: Black's knight on d5 has been shifted around several times and now stands strong. White shouldn't chase it with a flashy attack; instead, develop the queenside knight, supporting the center and getting ready to push the d-pawn.

hp-6ch.spoken: If Black faces Nd2, the best reply is h6, forcing the bishop back to h4, then c5, heading toward a hedgehog setup with b6 and Bb7. Strong players reach this position often, and it typically ends in draws.

hp-6ce.spoken: White recaptures with the b-pawn, and Black’s main reply is …b6, aiming the bishop at b7 along the long diagonal. White answers with Bd3, and once Black plays …d6 and castles, we arrive at the key Chase Variation position.

hp-6d6.spoken: White pins the knight with the bishop on g5, a classic aggressive setup, then challenges the center with the e-pawn.

hp-6d1.spoken: Black's queenside majority of two to one creates a potential passed pawn, but White's d5 pawn sits only three squares from promotion, making it the bigger threat.

hp-6d2.spoken: The Grünfeld is an imbalanced fight: White storms the center with e4 and d5, and exchange sacrifices can tip the game into sharp, fast finishes or favorable endgames for either side.

hp-6cm.spoken: White pushes e5, and the structure looks like a French. Black needs h6 to bother the bishop, but it drops back to e3. White's queenside knight hasn't moved, so the extra tempo fuels a kingside attack with f4.

hp-6d4.spoken: In the Grünfeld, this exchange variation is the critical main line. White gets a central pawn majority, while Black gains active piece play.

hp-6d8.spoken: White delays Nc3 to play g3 first, and Black answers with d5. That defines the Neo-Grünfeld, giving White's bishop on g2 more scope.

hp-6d5.spoken: The Russian system starts when White plays Qb3, skipping the exchange and pressuring Black's d5 pawn, which creates a different type of center.

hp-6cz.spoken: In the Grünfeld, Black holds off castling to hit the center at once with c5, targeting the d4 pawn. White’s center is wide but sits two tempi from castling; Black needs only one, and that gap fuels the imbalance.

hp-6d7.spoken: The Brinckmann attack brings the bishop to f4, but here that bishop supports the e-pawn and gives White a firmer center.

hp-6d9.spoken: The Grünfeld is a highly theoretical opening, so memorizing every variation is not realistic.

hp-6ev.spoken: White castles queenside and pushes the kingside pawns, f4 and g3 supporting the storm. The position stays balanced, but White’s attack carries real potential.

hp-6er.spoken: In the Anti-Moscow, Black keeps the extra pawn, but the structure becomes awkward and hard to manage. Dynamic chances run high, and Black must avoid overextending.

hp-6eh.spoken: The tension between the c-pawn and d5 is the heart of the Semi-Slav. Whether Black captures on c4 or not decides the character of the game. If he takes and holds the pawn, White gets sharp compensation.

hp-6e2.spoken: If Black plays Nc6 and then offers the trade of light-squared bishops, the b7 weakness gets solved, but it leaves White slightly better, since White's bishop was the stronger piece.

hp-6ep.spoken: White can sidestep both the Meran and Anti-Meran by playing Bg5, steering into some of the most tangled positions in the game.

hp-6ek.spoken: Taking the pawn on c4 comes with tempo, since White's bishop on d3 hangs. That is the key difference from putting the bishop on e2, where the same capture gains no tempo.

hp-6f5.spoken: Black has three main options here: b6, O-O, or Ne5. The b6 line plans a fianchetto, putting the light-squared bishop on b7 to pressure e4 and the long diagonal.

hp-6ex.spoken: Black’s queen on f6 aims at f2 and b2 while White’s king remains in the center. The direct Qxf2 check is not crushing, but it keeps White unsettled.

hp-6ef.spoken: The queen to a4 combined with the pawn to a4 is the standard treatment of the …Nc6 line, forcing a sequence both players must know cold. The endgame that follows becomes the real battleground, where preparation decides everything.

hp-6dv.spoken: In the line with Nc6, a tactical trick exists. If Black's knight lands on the rook, White answers with Ne1. If Black takes the rook, the knight is trapped and loses two pieces for it, showing White's edge.

hp-6es.spoken: The bishop on c5 is Black's strongest piece, eyeing the center and the kingside. White commonly challenges it with Be3.

hp-6el.spoken: If White delays the bishop and plays b3, Black can't grab on c4 right away, since the bishop still sits on f1. White holds it back to keep the tension and avoid handing Black a tempo.

hp-6e7.spoken: White can hold off castling here and play Kd2 instead, a more active square that keeps the king safe while aiming at c7 and the black king.

hp-6dy.spoken: After …Nc6, Qa4 is White's most practical weapon. It pressures the knight and prepares to win the c4-pawn, keeping a lasting slight edge without heavy theory.

hp-6f6.spoken: In the main line, Black plays b6, then White castles and Black develops the bishop to b7. White’s pawns on f4 and e4 are powerful, while Black’s bishops on c5 and b7 aim straight at the white king, backed by the queen on f6.

hp-6e6.spoken: If Black drops the bishop to d6, White takes the c-pawn with the knight and doubles the pawns. Then Bf4 hits c7, and the knight on d6 is misplaced, forced to move and leaves c4 undefended.

hp-6f9.spoken: The queen’s early trip to f6 leaves the bishop on c5 hanging and the c7 square weak — this position is tactically loaded.

hp-6fj.spoken: White plays h4, Black answers h5, and then White pushes e6. If Black takes on e6, weaknesses appear on d5 and f7 for White to attack. The engine calls it roughly equal, but Black has a hard time handling it.

hp-6fb.spoken: Black faces three main paths on move five in the Classical Scotch, and White chooses which one to play, so Black must know all three.

hp-6fh.spoken: If Black pulls the bishop back to g6, White can play f3, preparing both a queen move to h4 and a later f4 push. That move also keeps White's knight out of f3 for now.

hp-6ff.spoken: White's g5 pushes the knight to f5, where it rests strong and hard to chase off. No need for g6 to shield it — that wastes a tempo and shuts the square.

hp-6fk.spoken: If Black takes on e6, White plays bishop d3, forcing the queen to recapture. Then White's queen goes to g6 with threats, and Black must be exact to survive.

hp-6gc.spoken: The queen check on a4 works because if Black blocks with c6, White pushes d5. If Black takes, the knight recaptures, and the queen on a4 guards the e4 pawn. With the queen still on d1, that pawn would be left undefended and Black could target it.

hp-6fl.spoken: The engine's first choice after e6 is hxg4, but that leads to a messy position where Black has to push e5 to get developed. White can stop that with queen g5, and Black must go e6 — a tight, cramped setup.

hp-6ga.spoken: Retreating the bishop to f8 looks passive but is actually a solid defensive setup. White's reply is d4, opening the center.

hp-6ge.spoken: Black can decline the Evans Gambit by pulling the bishop back to e7 and castling — a solid choice that sidesteps the sharp lines but gives White a measure of initiative.

hp-6g5.spoken: White sacrifices a pawn for active piece play, a gambit proven sound at the highest level. If Black declines with Bb6, White keeps a comfortable space edge on the queenside.

hp-6fn.spoken: Early f4 is wrong in the queen d6 line because Black's light-squared bishop is still active and can trade itself off, then Black plays e6 and attacks the f4 pawn with the knight jumping e7-g6.

hp-6g8.spoken: White plays c3 to prepare d4 and seize space; Black's bishop has five retreat squares, each starting a different line.

hp-6g3.spoken: The Bayonet Attack is a sharp, faster take on the Caro-Kann Advance, mixing Tal and Van der Wiel ideas. Black can take the pawn on g4 with the bishop at once, but White gains fast development and attacking chances.

hp-6gg.spoken: White reaches a critical moment here. If he defends d4 passively with Qf4, Black is fine. But the sharper Rfe1 allows Black to take on d4, and the game becomes extremely sharp with chances for both sides.

hp-6fg.spoken: Black can pick a French-style setup or keep the Caro-Kann character. The bishop usually lands on g6, and the idea of Bf5-e4 invites White to play f3, a move White often wants anyway.

hp-6fo.spoken: In this Caro-Kann Advance, that bishop on f5 is central. If White advances f4, the bishop gets locked in, which favors Black. White instead steers the f4 square with pieces, letting the e-pawn stand and leaving Black at ease.

hp-6fa.spoken: In the main line, White's e-pawn stays a lasting weakness. The black queen looks active but accomplishes little, while the minor pieces remain locked in sharp central tension.

hp-6hf.spoken: White's last move, Be3, completes the forced sequence of the Steinitz Variation in the Classical French.

hp-6hr.spoken: Black's plan on this side of the board is to push b5 and start a queenside attack. First the c6 knight must move so the bishop on d7 can guard that pawn.

hp-6go.spoken: White is down a pawn, seven to eight, but the activity and piece play give compensation. If the initiative is not converted, the material deficit will tell.

hp-6ht.spoken: After the captures resolve, White comes out a pawn ahead, but Black's bishop pair and attacking threats give real compensation. The engine may favor White slightly, but Black's attack is far easier to play in practice.

hp-6gm.spoken: If Black castles and then captures on e4, White takes back with the d-pawn, and after the exchanges, Qd5 wins material—Black's pieces are overloaded.

hp-6h1.spoken: White must not take on e5, because Black recaptures with the bishop and gets a slightly better position. Instead, Qb6 is strong, hitting the knight and piling on pressure.

hp-6gu.spoken: In this critical spot after Nf6, the most combative try is Nb5, sacrificing the rook for sharp play. Black answers with d5, guarding c7 and hitting the bishop, leaving Black's rooks idle while White's pieces hum with activity.

hp-6hn.spoken: With the bishop on d7, Black covers the c6-knight, so if White takes it, Black recaptures and keeps the balance. An immediate d5 break fails here, because White has enough defenders around the king.

hp-6gk.spoken: White castles first to keep the attack rolling, and Black plays d6 to shore up the center. The pawn takes back on d4, kicking the bishop, which lands on b6—passive and locked in behind the d4 pawn.

hp-6gn.spoken: Black can't safely take on e4 here, because White answers with Qd5 or Qd4, attacking both knights. So after castling, that pawn on e4 isn’t a real target.

hp-6gr.spoken: In the Lasker Defense, once the queens come off, Black keeps the healthier pawn structure. White’s a2 and c4 pawns become targets, and the bishop on b6 stands strong. Defending the e4 pawn is a real problem.

hp-6gz.spoken: After Black plays a6, they're ready to push b5 and start a queenside expansion, a standard French setup. White answers best with Qd2, reinforcing the center and getting ready for Rd1, while Black's f8-bishop still has no comfortable home.

hp-6hs.spoken: After Black plays b5, White must respond quickly with h4 and a4 to build counterplay. The position turns razor-sharp, both sides racing to attack. A zwischenzug like Bxf6 can appear, taking the knight to break Black's coordination.

hp-6hb.spoken: Black should take on e5 rather than play f5. Capturing leaves White with a weak isolated e-pawn, gives Black an outpost on e4, and sets up pressure on the d5 pawn.

hp-6gv.spoken: White gives up the rook on a1, yet the activity of his pieces balances the ledger, while Black's rooks sit passive on a8 and h8. The engine calls this roughly equal, maybe a touch better for Black.

hp-6ie.spoken: If White tries Bg5, Black answers with e6. If White goes Nc3, Black plays g6 — a key branching point.

hp-6hz.spoken: In this critical position, White should not take on b5. Play g5 instead to keep pushing the kingside attack. Black answers with h5 or other ideas to stir up counterplay.

hp-6i9.spoken: White's key idea here is the Maroczy Bind, with the light-squared bishop already traded off—and that bishop is often a liability.

hp-6iq.spoken: This anti-Sicilian approach with Bb5 or Bc4 sidesteps mainline Open Sicilian theory and pushes Black to make choices early. It's a practical weapon that trims the theory White has to prepare.

hp-6io.spoken: If Black leaves the bishop on g7, White can play Bg5, hitting the e7 pawn. Black must deal with that threat immediately, because ignoring it or castling allows Bxe7.

hp-6i2.spoken: This position is razor sharp and heavily theorized, with countless grandmaster games. Under 2300, it's often smarter to steer away from the most critical lines and pick a more solid setup.

hp-6iy.spoken: If Black pokes with h6, take on f6 and let Black recapture with the g-pawn. White gets a weak h6-pawn to target, and the position takes on a Caro-Kann flavor.

hp-6is.spoken: The Veresov works best against opponents unfamiliar with it, especially King's Indian players. They may not expect Nc3 and the push e2-e4, so White steers the game into unknown territory.

hp-6i8.spoken: If White plays the knight instead of Bg5, Black fianchettoes with g6 and Bg7, reaching a Dragon-style Maroczy Bind setup.

hp-6id.spoken: Black has a solid, Dragon-style setup here.

hp-6iv.spoken: If Black plays e6, White replies e4, turning the game into the French Defense, the Burn Variation. This mainline has thousands of games behind it, so White needs to be ready.

hp-6hy.spoken: Black can try b5, offering a pawn to pull the bishop away and open lines toward the white king. If White takes it, Black gains active pieces and real attacking chances.

hp-6j3.spoken: If White captures on f6 and Black retakes with the e-pawn, that g6 pawn becomes a real problem in this Caro-Kann setup — it leaves the kingside fragile and shuts off the knight's route to f8 and g6.

hp-6hw.spoken: The dark-squared bishop on e3 guards the kingside. Black wants to swap it off with a knight, forcing bishop takes and rook takes back, to blunt White's attack.

hp-6ic.spoken: If White plays Bg5 instead of Nc3, Black’s reply changes.

hp-6im.spoken: The bishop on c8 has yet to develop. The engine may call this equal, but White wants more, since Bc4 on move five usually yields a slight edge.

hp-6if.spoken: White's setup mirrors a Maroczy Bind, with the bishop on c4 playing its typical role.

hp-6i4.spoken: If White castles before playing Bc4, Black gets an immediate d5 in the center, seizing counterplay right away. This is the critical crossroads of the main line.

hp-6k1.spoken: Black's g6 gives White a hook on the kingside — the target for h4-h5, prying open lines against the castled king. Before g6, that attack would be slow and expensive.

hp-6jo.spoken: Black has five solid replies here: h6, c6, e6, e5, or g6. Each one steers the game in a very different direction.

hp-6jx.spoken: Playing Bd3 here is too passive. It breaks the pin but creates no real pressure. Black simply plays d6, and the resulting structure is Slav-like, with easy equality.

hp-6ji.spoken: If Black plays h6 to kick the bishop, White retreats to h4. After e6, White can push e4, transposing into a Rubinstein French — a good choice for a player who knows that line. Otherwise, playing e3 leaves White slightly worse.

hp-6kh.spoken: The move f3 is the soul of the Yugoslav Attack. It builds a pawn chain that props up the center and clears the way for a kingside storm. Skip it, and the game drifts into calmer waters like the Classical or Levenfish lines, where White’s attack loses its bite.

hp-6js.spoken: If Black plays e6, White answers with e4, and after dxe4 the knight recaptures, giving a French-style setup. The position is ordinary, and White can castle queenside and start an attack.

hp-6jc.spoken: Black must castle, since the knight to f6 is unavailable and other development leaves White pressing. If Black develops cleanly, he gets a favorable Caro-Kann structure and stands better.

hp-6jw.spoken: After Nb5, Black must not take the pawn on e4. The bishop on c5 is under attack, and g7 is also exposed — a queen landing on g3 hits both. The Qg4 try is still insufficient.
